title: How Long Do Dental Implants Take? Timeline and Guide

description: Dental implants take about 3 months in ideal cases and 6 to 12 months with grafting. Each phase explained, with what speeds or slows it, in Valencia.

keyTakeaways: Implant treatment commonly takes about 3 months for ideal immediate-placement cases and 6 to 12 months when grafting and staged healing are needed.
Osseointegration, the bone bonding to the implant, takes 3 to 6 months and accounts for most of the timeline.
Bone grafts and sinus lifts add roughly 3 to 6 months before the implant can be placed.
Immediate loading gives you a tooth the same day but suits only sites with good bone, no infection and firm implant stability.
Stopping smoking, controlling diabetes and following instructions are the safest ways to keep your timeline short.
body:
## From start to finish

How long [dental implants](/services/dental-implants/) take is the first question most patients ask once they decide to replace a missing tooth. The direct answer: treatment commonly runs about **3 months** for ideal immediate-placement cases and **6 to 12 months** when staged grafting and healing are needed. A precise timetable depends on your bone, any infection, and the goal, whether a single crown or a full-arch restoration. Dr. Nuriel Lavi at Valencia Dentistry maps that timeline from a CBCT scan at your consultation; our [first visit guide](/why-choose-valencia-smile-what-to-expect-on-your-first-visit/) explains how planning works.

## Why the timeline varies

Different parts of implant treatment move at different speeds. Three drivers explain most of the variation:

- **Biology:** bone healing (osseointegration) sets the pace in most cases.
- **Surgical complexity:** extractions, grafts or sinus lifts add time.
- **Restorative goals:** an immediate provisional tooth shortens the visible wait, but the final restoration still waits for stable integration.

Dr. Lavi puts long-term predictability ahead of speed. A tooth can often be provided quickly, but rushing a compromised site raises the risk of complications.

## Typical timelines by approach

These benchmarks assume a healthy patient without major medical contraindications.

| Approach | Typical stages | Usual timeline | When a visible tooth appears |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Immediate implant with provisional** | Extraction, implant placed the same day, provisional crown, final crown after integration | 3–4 months to final crown | Same day (provisional) |
| **Staged implant with grafting** | Extraction, bone graft, healing, implant placement, integration, final crown | 6–12+ months | Temporary denture or flipper during healing |
| **All-on-4 or full-arch immediate load** | Extractions, several implants placed, fixed provisional the same day, final prosthesis after integration | 3–6 months to final prosthesis | Same day (fixed provisional) |

## Each phase, and why it takes the time it does

### 1. Evaluation and planning (1–3 weeks)

We start with your medical history, an exam and a 3D CBCT scan to assess bone volume, anatomy and sinus position. Digital planning sets the implant size and position and predicts whether grafting will be needed. Thorough diagnostics up front reduce surprises later.

### 2. Extraction and socket healing (4–12 weeks when needed)

After an extraction, the gum closes within weeks, but bone remodels more slowly. In a clean socket we may place the implant immediately; if infection or bone loss is present, we usually wait 6–12 weeks or place a socket preservation graft, which heals over about 3 months.

### 3. Bone grafting or sinus lift (3–6+ months)

Grafts restore width or height so the implant has solid support. Small grafts can heal in roughly three months; larger vertical augmentations or lateral sinus lifts commonly need four to six months. Material and technique influence healing time.

### 4. Implant surgery (one appointment)

Placement is an outpatient procedure that usually takes 30–90 minutes per implant. With guided surgery and high initial stability, we may attach a provisional for immediate function; otherwise the site is closed and left to integrate undisturbed.

### 5. Osseointegration (3–6 months)

Osseointegration is the biological bond between bone and the implant surface, and it accounts for most of the timeline. Lower-jaw sites often integrate in about 3 months; upper-jaw bone is usually less dense and may need 4–6 months. Modern implant surfaces have shortened integration times, but conservative healing gives the most predictable long-term result. Systematic reviews report 5-year survival above 90 percent in well-selected cases.

### 6. Abutment and final restoration (2–6 weeks)

After integration we attach an abutment and take digital impressions with the iTero scanner. A single crown is quick to fabricate; bridges and full-arch prostheses need extra time for try-ins and adjustments. This step restores full chewing function.

### 7. Maintenance (ongoing)

Regular recall visits and professional cleaning keep implants healthy. An early X-ray after restoration and then annual checks catch bone changes around the implant before they become irreversible.

## Immediate loading versus a staged approach

Immediate loading is appealing because you leave with a tooth, but it works best when conditions are right: adequate bone, no active infection and good implant stability at placement. Staged treatment trades time for predictability.

| Feature | Immediate loading | Staged approach |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Time to a visible tooth | Same day | Weeks to months (temporary denture possible) |
| Predictability in compromised sites | Lower | Higher |
| Need for grafting | Less common, site-dependent | Often required before the implant |

## Success rates and risk factors

Modern implant dentistry reports high long-term survival: most published series show five-year survival above **90 to 95 percent** in healthy patients when implants are placed and restored appropriately. Risk rises with smoking, uncontrolled diabetes, poor oral hygiene and previous radiation to the head and neck. Dr. Lavi reviews these risks with you plainly so you can address them before surgery, for example by stopping smoking or improving blood sugar control.

## Three realistic scenarios

1. **Front tooth, good bone:** extraction with immediate implant and provisional; final crown at about 3 months.
2. **Molar with bone loss:** socket graft (3 months), implant placement, 3 months of integration, then the crown; about 7–9 months in all.
3. **Full-arch rehabilitation:** remaining teeth removed and four implants placed with a fixed provisional; final prosthesis at 3–6 months.

## How to shorten your timeline safely

Optimize what you can control: stop smoking before surgery, manage diabetes, follow pre- and post-operative instructions, and keep your mouth clean. CBCT planning and digital workflows also reduce appointments and lab time. If speed matters to you, say so; we will outline immediate versus staged options and the relative risks.

## What can extend the timeline

- **Persistent infection:** may require antibiotics, drainage, or staged extraction and healing before placement.
- **Graft failure or slow integration:** calls for removal, re-grafting and additional healing.
- **Peri-implantitis:** early treatment helps, but advanced disease may require implant removal and reconstruction.

## Checklist before you book

- Bring a list of your medications and your medical history.
- Ask for a CBCT-guided plan that shows staging and realistic timelines.
- Confirm whether you will have a temporary tooth during healing.
- Discuss financing and the total cost for staged versus immediate options.

## Next step

Your timeline depends on anatomy, infection status, grafting needs and whether immediate or staged loading is right for you. Expect about three months for ideal immediate protocols and six to twelve months when grafting is involved. The reliable way to know your own timeline is a CBCT-guided consultation with a written plan, timeline and estimate. faq.q: How long until I can eat normally after implant surgery?
faq.a: Expect soft foods for the first week, and avoid heavy biting on a new provisional for several weeks. Once the final restoration is in place and integration is confirmed, you can return to a normal diet. Recovery varies with the extent of surgery and any grafting.

faq.q: Will I always need a bone graft?
faq.a: No. If there is adequate bone at the site, grafting is unnecessary. When the ridge is too thin or the sinus sits too low for a stable implant, a graft or sinus lift is needed for long-term stability.

faq.q: Can implants fail after the crown is placed?
faq.a: Yes, though failure after restoration is uncommon with proper maintenance. Peri-implantitis, an infection around the implant, is the most frequent cause and can lead to bone loss if untreated. Regular professional care and daily hygiene reduce the risk.

In carefully selected cases with good bone and firm initial stability, yes. It requires precise surgical and prosthetic execution. Published trials show success rates comparable to delayed loading when the selection criteria are met.

faq.q: How often should implants be checked after placement?
faq.a: Follow-ups typically happen at 1 to 2 weeks after surgery, again at 3 to 6 months, and then annually. Periodic X-rays help detect early bone changes. Patients with a history of gum disease or other risk factors may need more frequent maintenance.

faq.q: What is the cost difference between immediate and staged implants?
faq.a: It depends on complexity and whether grafts or multiple implants are needed. Immediate protocols can reduce some lab and appointment fees but may require specialized components. We provide a written estimate after the CBCT and planning visit so you can compare both options.
